title: Primary Structural Function
learningObjectives: Describe the bracket's structural role.
student: What is the primary structural function of the offset bracket?
instructor: It transfers forces from the lower actuator or linkage and suspended load into the machine frame while providing geometric clearance for adjacent equipment.

title: External Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the forces entering the bracket.
student: Identify the externally applied loads that enter the bracket through the lower joint.
instructor: A horizontal force F enters from the actuator or linkage, and a vertical force P enters from the suspended tooling or restraint load.

title: Upper Attachment Role
learningObjectives: Explain the role and scope of the upper attachment.
student: What role does the upper bolted connection play in the load path?
instructor: It transfers the bracket reaction forces and moments into the structural frame. Detailed bolt, bearing, and connection stresses are outside the base problem.

title: Load Path to the Frame
learningObjectives: Trace both loads through the assembly.
student: Trace the load path from the actuator and suspended tooling to the final support.
instructor: Actuator and suspended-load forces pass through the lower pin into the offset bracket, then through the upper bolted attachment into the overhead machine frame.

title: Section a-a as a Critical Location
learningObjectives: Explain why the selected section is useful for nominal stress analysis.
student: Why is section a-a useful for evaluating the bracket's local nominal stress state?
instructor: The section lies in the vertical leg above the lower pin and must carry the combined internal axial force, transverse shear, and bending moment generated by the eccentric lower-joint loads.

title: Expected Stress Components
learningObjectives: Select the stress components needed at the section.
student: Which stress components should be considered at section a-a?
instructor: Consider uniform normal stress from axial force, linearly varying normal stress from bending, and transverse shear stress associated with the horizontal shear force.

title: Relevant Geometry
learningObjectives: Identify geometry entering the lower-section stress calculation.
student: Which dimensions control the stress calculation at A and B, and which shown dimension does not enter the selected lower-segment cut?
instructor: Section width b, thickness t, vertical lever arm h, and horizontal eccentricity c control the calculation. Upper offset e describes the overall geometry but does not enter equilibrium of the isolated portion below section a-a.

title: Student-Generated Section-Cut FBD
learningObjectives: Create the lower-segment free-body diagram.
student: Before viewing the reference idealization, isolate the bracket portion below section a-a. Show F and P at the lower joint, dimensions h and c, and internal resultants N, V, and M at the cut. Define your force and moment sign conventions.
instructor: A valid FBD shows horizontal F acting left, vertical P acting downward, perpendicular moment arms h and c, and a statically equivalent axial force, transverse shear, and couple at section a-a.
gradingNotes: Students should create the lower-segment cut before seeing the instructor reference idealization.
commonMistakes: Do not include upper-connection reactions on a free body that contains only the material below section a-a.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions defining the model's scope.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real bracket assembly into the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Assume static concentrated loads, a prismatic rectangular member at section a-a, small deformation, and linear-elastic nominal-stress formulas. Neglect self-weight, local pin and contact effects, bend and hole stress concentrations, connector flexibility, fatigue, and detailed upper-bolt behavior.

title: Combined-Stress Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the complete section and stress analysis.
student: List the calculation sequence needed to determine and compare the stress states at A and B.
instructor: Use lower-segment equilibrium to find N, V, and M; calculate A and Iz; compute uniform axial and extreme-fiber bending stress; superpose the normal stresses at A and B; evaluate transverse shear at those points; draw stress elements; and compare absolute normal-stress magnitudes.

title: Axial Force and Transverse Shear
learningObjectives: Determine internal forces from a section-cut FBD.
student: Using the portion below section a-a, determine the internal axial force N and transverse shear V. State their physical senses.
instructor: N = P = {{act_N_lb}} lb in tension. The transverse-shear magnitude is V = F = {{act_V_lb}} lb. The force senses on the exposed cut must oppose the applied lower-joint forces.

title: Internal Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Calculate the signed internal moment using perpendicular lever arms.
student: Determine the internal bending moment at section a-a. Take counterclockwise moment on the lower segment as positive and explain whether the two applied-force moments reinforce or oppose.
instructor: The horizontal-force contribution is Fh = {{act_MF_lbin}} lb·in, while the vertical-force contribution is Pc = {{act_MP_lbin}} lb·in in the opposite sense. Therefore M = Fh - Pc = {{act_M_lbin}} lb·in {{act_M_direction}}, with magnitude {{act_M_abs_lbin}} lb·in.
gradingNotes: Require perpendicular moment arms: h for F and c for P. Offset e is not part of this cut.

title: Rectangular Section Properties
learningObjectives: Calculate area and centroidal moment of inertia in the bending direction.
student: Determine the cross-sectional area A, extreme-fiber coordinate, and centroidal second moment of area Iz for bending across width b.
instructor: A = bt = {{act_area_in2}} in2. Points A and B are at |x| = b/2 = {{act_x_extreme_in}} in. The required centroidal property is Iz = tb3/12 = {{act_I_in4}} in4.
commonMistakes: Width b is cubed because bending stress varies across b in the shown model.

title: Uniform Axial Normal Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate the axial normal-stress contribution.
student: Determine the uniform normal stress caused by axial force N.
instructor: σN = N/A = {{act_sigma_N_psi}} psi = {{act_sigma_N_ksi}} ksi in tension.

title: Extreme-Fiber Bending Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate the signed bending contribution at the two surfaces.
student: Determine the bending-stress magnitude at extreme points A and B using the flexure formula. State which side receives bending tension for your moment sign.
instructor: The magnitude is |σb| = |M|(b/2)/Iz = {{act_sigma_b_psi}} psi = {{act_sigma_b_ksi}} ksi. For a positive counterclockwise internal moment on the lower segment, A receives bending compression and B receives bending tension; the senses reverse if M is negative.

title: Combined Normal Stress at A
learningObjectives: Superpose axial and bending stress at point A.
student: Combine the axial and bending contributions to determine the signed normal stress at point A.
instructor: Using tension as positive, σA = σN - M(b/2)/Iz = {{act_sigma_A_psi}} psi = {{act_sigma_A_ksi}} ksi. Point A is in {{act_sigma_A_type}}.

title: Combined Normal Stress at B
learningObjectives: Superpose axial and bending stress at point B.
student: Combine the axial and bending contributions to determine the signed normal stress at point B.
instructor: Using tension as positive, σB = σN + M(b/2)/Iz = {{act_sigma_B_psi}} psi = {{act_sigma_B_ksi}} ksi. Point B is in {{act_sigma_B_type}}.

title: Transverse Shear at A and B
learningObjectives: Evaluate shear at surface points and at the centroid.
student: Determine the transverse shear stress caused by V at points A and B. Also calculate the maximum rectangular-section transverse shear for reference.
instructor: Because A and B lie on the side free surfaces at x = ±b/2, τA = {{act_tau_A_psi}} psi and τB = {{act_tau_B_psi}} psi. The parabolic distribution reaches τmax = 3V/(2A) = {{act_tau_max_psi}} psi = {{act_tau_max_ksi}} ksi at the centroid.
commonMistakes: Using the average V/A or maximum 1.5V/A value at a side free surface is incorrect.

title: Stress Elements at A and B
learningObjectives: Translate calculated components into differential stress elements.
student: Sketch differential stress elements at A and B and label the stress magnitudes and senses.
instructor: At A, draw a uniaxial {{act_sigma_A_type}} normal stress of signed value {{act_sigma_A_ksi}} ksi and zero transverse shear at the surface. At B, draw a uniaxial {{act_sigma_B_type}} normal stress of signed value {{act_sigma_B_ksi}} ksi and zero transverse shear at the surface.

title: Critical Point and Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Identify the governing surface and recommend a mechanics-based modification.
student: Identify the more critical point for normal-stress magnitude, recommend one geometric change that would reduce bending demand, and state at least three limitations requiring later analysis.
instructor: {{act_assessment}}
gradingNotes: The recommendation must distinguish changes to moment arms from changes to section properties.
commonMistakes: Do not claim the complete bracket is safe from nominal stress at one section alone.
